brown-throated-sloth.anatomy: The brown-throated sloth has a round head, a flat face with a dark mask across its eyes, and, as its name says, a brown throat. Its shaggy, greyish-brown fur grows in the opposite direction to most mammals', parting along the belly and running toward the back, so rain runs off while it hangs upside-down. Each hair has cracks in which algae grow. It has three long, curved claws on each limb, up to about 10 centimetres, that hook over branches so firmly that sloths can hang, and even sleep, with little effort; some have been found still hanging after death. It has roughly 30 percent less muscle than you would expect for an animal its size, which reduces its energy needs. Its body temperature changes with the weather more than most mammals', falling at night and rising as it basks in the morning sun.
brown-throated-sloth.family: Brown-throated sloths live alone, each with a home range of a few trees. Females call with a shrill, high-pitched scream, a sound like 'ay-ee', to attract males when ready to mate. After a pregnancy of about six months, the female gives birth to a single baby while hanging in the trees. The baby clings to her belly and travels with her for around six months, learning which leaves to eat by licking them from her lips. As it grows, it begins to eat on its own. When it leaves, the mother often hands over part of her home range to her offspring, and young sloths may stay nearby. Sloths grow slowly and reach maturity at around three years. In the wild, their main predators are harpy eagles, jaguars and ocelots.
brown-throated-sloth.people: Sloths have long puzzled and charmed people. Early European naturalists described them as lazy and badly designed, an idea scientists have since overturned: they are superbly adapted to a low-energy life. In recent years, sloths have become internet stars, and sanctuaries in Costa Rica and Panama care for orphaned and injured sloths, many hurt by power lines, dogs or traffic. Conservation groups build rope 'sloth crossings' over roads, insulate power lines and plant trees to reconnect forest patches. The pet trade is a growing problem, as people pay to take selfies with captive sloths, which can be stressful for these shy animals. Tourists can help by choosing responsible wildlife experiences that do not involve holding sloths. Scientists also study sloth fur, which hosts unique fungi and microbes that may lead to new medicines.

jaguar.anatomy: The jaguar is a stocky, muscular cat with a broad head, powerful jaws and short, thick legs, built for strength rather than long chases. Its golden coat is covered in black rosettes, most with one or more dots in the centre, and some jaguars are almost entirely black, a colour form called melanistic, though their rosettes still show in sunlight. Its canine teeth are long and its bite force exceptional for its size, strong enough to pierce turtle shells and the thick skulls of caimans. Large paws with sharp, retractable claws help it grip prey and climb trees. Jaguars have excellent night vision and hearing, and are confident swimmers with a stocky build suited to wading through wetlands. Their call is a deep, repeated grunt, often compared to the sound of a saw cutting wood.
jaguar.family: Jaguars are solitary. Males have large territories that may overlap with those of several females, and both sexes mark their areas with scratches, urine and scent. When a female is ready to breed, she calls more often to attract males, and the pair stays together for a few days. After about three and a half months, she gives birth in a den, often among rocks, dense vegetation or a riverbank cave, to usually one to four cubs, which are blind at first. They begin to follow her at around two months and learn to hunt by watching and practising. Cubs stay with their mother for about two years before leaving to establish their own territories. Young males often travel far, and this is when many come into conflict with people.
jaguar.people: The jaguar was a powerful symbol for many civilisations of the Americas. The Olmec, Maya and Aztecs linked it to royalty, warfare and the underworld; Aztec elite warriors were known as jaguar warriors, and Maya rulers wore jaguar skins. In the 20th century, jaguars were heavily hunted for their fur, until international trade was banned in the 1970s. Today they are threatened by deforestation and by ranchers who kill them for preying on cattle. Conservation groups such as Panthera work with ranchers to protect herds using better fencing, guard animals and compensation, and promote jaguar tourism, especially in Brazil's Pantanal, where visitors can see them hunting along rivers. The Jaguar Corridor Initiative aims to keep populations connected from Mexico to Argentina, and jaguars occasionally still wander into the southern United States.

andean-condor.anatomy: The Andean condor is a huge, black vulture with white patches on its wings and a ruff of white feathers around the base of its neck. Its head and neck are bare and greyish to reddish, an advantage for a bird that feeds inside carcasses, since bare skin stays cleaner; the skin can flush or change colour with the bird's mood. Males have a large, fleshy comb on their forehead and a wattle on their neck. Unlike most birds of prey, males are larger than females. Its feet are relatively weak and not built for grasping, so it cannot carry prey; instead, it uses its strong, hooked beak to tear through tough hides. Its huge wings have long, separated primary feathers at the tips, which act like fingers to reduce turbulence and help it soar on rising air.
andean-condor.family: Andean condors usually mate for life. Courtship involves the male puffing out his neck, spreading his wings, hissing and clicking. Pairs nest on high, inaccessible cliff ledges or in caves, usually without building much of a nest, and the female lays a single egg every second year. Both parents take turns incubating it for about two months, then feed the chick by regurgitating food. The young condor can fly at around six months, but it stays with its parents and is fed by them for up to two years. Condors take a long time to grow up: they gain their adult colours and begin breeding at around six to eight years old. Their slow pace means that every death of an adult has a big effect on the population.
andean-condor.people: The Andean condor has been a sacred bird for Andean peoples for thousands of years; Inca beliefs linked it to the upper world and the heavens, and it remains a symbol of strength and freedom. It appears on the coats of arms of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia and Ecuador and in countless songs and festivals, including the famous Peruvian tune 'El Cóndor Pasa'. Yet condors have declined, especially in the northern Andes, poisoned by baits left for pumas and foxes, by lead from bullets in carcasses, and occasionally shot. Zoos in North and South America breed condors, and since the late 1980s captive-raised birds have been released in Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and elsewhere, often raised with condor puppets so they don't become used to humans, an approach first developed for the related California condor.

marine-iguana.anatomy: Marine iguanas are stocky lizards with blunt, rounded snouts, a crest of spines along their backs and long, flattened tails. Their blunt faces and sharp, three-pointed teeth help them scrape algae off rocks. Most are black or dark grey, which helps them absorb heat from the sun after cold swims, although some populations turn red, green or turquoise in the breeding season. Their strong, sharp claws let them cling to rocks against crashing waves. In the water, they swim by swinging their flattened tail from side to side, holding their legs against their bodies. To dive in cold water, they slow their heart rate to save oxygen. Special salt glands above their eyes remove excess salt from the blood, which they sneeze out, leaving their heads crusted with white salt.
marine-iguana.family: In the breeding season, males defend small territories on the shore, bobbing their heads and fighting rivals by pushing head to head. Large males with the best territories mate with many females. A few weeks after mating, females move to sandy areas, sometimes inland, and dig burrows to lay one to six eggs, then guard the nest site for a few days before leaving. The eggs incubate in the warm sand for about three to four months. Hatchlings dig their way out and must avoid predators such as Galápagos hawks, herons and snakes as they head toward the shore. Young marine iguanas feed on algae in the shallows and grow slowly. When food is plentiful they can live for decades.
marine-iguana.people: Charles Darwin found marine iguanas fascinating and somewhat repulsive when he visited the Galápagos in 1835. He tested their swimming and diving and noted that they never seemed to flee into the sea when threatened, preferring to stay on land. Their adaptations to an ocean diet later became a classic example of evolution. Today they are protected within Galápagos National Park and the Galápagos Marine Reserve. Their main threats come from introduced animals such as cats, dogs and rats, oil spills, and El Niño events, which warm the water, kill algae and can cause mass starvation. Scientists monitor iguana populations as an indicator of ocean health, and visitors who see them basking along the shore are asked to keep their distance and never feed them.

european-hedgehog.anatomy: The European hedgehog has a pointed face, small eyes, short legs and a coat of brown and cream spines on its back and sides, with coarse fur on its face and belly. Each spine is a hollow, stiffened hair, around 2 to 3 centimetres long, and is replaced over time; a hedgehog doesn't shoot or lose spines when threatened. A large muscle under the skin allows it to draw its head, legs and tail inside a prickly ball. Its eyesight is poor, but its senses of smell and hearing are excellent, and it uses its long snout to sniff out food under leaves and soil. Its many small, sharp teeth crunch beetles and other hard-bodied prey. Despite their short legs, hedgehogs can move surprisingly fast, climb walls and fences, and even swim.
european-hedgehog.family: Hedgehogs mate between April and September. Courtship can be noisy: a male circles a female for hours, snorting and huffing while she rebuffs him. After about five weeks, the female gives birth in a nest of leaves and grass to an average of four or five hoglets. They are born with soft, white spines covered by a membrane, which prevents injury to the mother; within hours the spines poke through. Hoglets open their eyes at about two weeks and start leaving the nest with their mother at about three weeks. They are weaned and independent at around six weeks. Late litters are in danger because young hedgehogs need to gain enough weight, roughly 450 to 600 grams, before winter to survive hibernation.
european-hedgehog.people: The hedgehog is one of Britain's best-loved wild animals, starring in Beatrix Potter's 'The Tale of Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle' and voted the UK's favourite species in several polls. It has been eaten in some places and appeared in folk tales, including the old belief that hedgehogs carried fruit on their spines. In the UK, hedgehog numbers have fallen sharply since the mid-20th century, especially in the countryside. The British Hedgehog Preservation Society and People's Trust for Endangered Species run Hedgehog Street, which encourages people to make holes in fences, leave wild corners, avoid slug pellets, check bonfires before lighting them, and check long grass before strimming or mowing. Volunteer rescue centres care for injured or underweight hedgehogs. Robotic lawnmowers have become a concern, prompting campaigns to avoid using them at night.

komodo-dragon.anatomy: The Komodo dragon is a massive monitor lizard with a long, heavy body, strong limbs, curved claws and a muscular tail. Its rough skin is reinforced with tiny bones called osteoderms, which act like chainmail. Its teeth are flattened and serrated like a shark's, designed to slice flesh, and are replaced throughout its life. Its jaw is relatively weak for its size, so it relies on its slashing bite, venom and the power of its neck and body to pull prey apart. Like snakes, it flicks its long, yellow, forked tongue to collect scent particles and passes them to a sensory organ in the roof of its mouth, letting it track dying animals or carcasses. It has good eyesight in daylight but poor night vision, and can run in short bursts at around 20 km/h.
komodo-dragon.family: Komodo dragons mate between May and August. Males compete by wrestling, standing up on their hind legs and grappling until one is pushed to the ground. In September, the female lays around 20 eggs, often in nests dug by megapode birds or in burrows on hillsides, and may guard the nest for months. The eggs take about seven to eight months to hatch, emerging around April when insects are plentiful. Hatchlings are around 40 centimetres long and immediately climb into trees, where they eat insects, geckos and birds, safe from adults that would eat them. Young dragons roll in faeces to smell unappetising. They spend several years in trees before moving to the ground. In zoos, some isolated females have produced offspring by parthenogenesis, all of which were male.
komodo-dragon.people: Stories of 'land crocodiles' on Indonesian islands reached Western scientists in the early 1900s, and the Komodo dragon was described in 1912 by Peter Ouwens, director of a zoological museum on Java. Its fearsome look helped inspire the 1933 film 'King Kong'. Local people on Komodo have a legend that the dragons are their siblings, descended from the same princess, and have lived alongside them for generations. Komodo National Park was created in 1980 and attracts tens of thousands of visitors a year, who can see dragons only with trained park rangers. Attacks on people are rare but have happened. Scientists study Komodo venom and their immune systems, and zoos around the world run breeding programs. Indonesia has debated limiting tourist numbers to protect the islands' fragile ecosystems.

peacock-mantis-shrimp.anatomy: The peacock mantis shrimp is one of the most colourful animals on coral reefs, with a green body, orange legs and bright, leopard-spotted front shield. Its most famous features are its two club-like raptorial appendages, folded under its head like a praying mantis's arms. A spring-like structure and a latch let it store energy and release it in a fraction of a millisecond, swinging the club with enormous force. The club's surface is made of a hard mineral layer over a structure of fibres arranged in a spiral, which stops cracks from spreading. Its eyes sit on stalks and each is divided into three regions, giving it depth perception in a single eye. Each eye has up to 16 types of photoreceptor, sensitive to ultraviolet and polarised light, though it may process colour very differently from us.
peacock-mantis-shrimp.family: Peacock mantis shrimp live in burrows they dig in sand and rubble, sometimes lining the entrance with stones and shells. Many mantis shrimp form long-lasting pairs, sharing a burrow. After mating, the female lays a mass of hundreds to thousands of eggs, which she carries under her body or keeps in the burrow, cleaning and aerating them for weeks. During this time she may eat very little. The eggs hatch into tiny, transparent larvae that drift in the plankton for weeks to months, growing through several stages before settling on the reef and becoming miniature adults. Peacock mantis shrimp can live for several years and molt regularly, regrowing damaged limbs and even replacing their clubs with fresh ones.
peacock-mantis-shrimp.people: In the aquarium world, mantis shrimp have a mixed reputation: some hobbyists treasure them, while others find a stowaway shrimp hidden in live rock smashing other animals and sometimes cracking the glass. Divers in the Indo-Pacific seek out the peacock mantis shrimp as a highlight of reef dives. Its powerful club has inspired engineers and materials scientists, who study its spiral fibre structure to design stronger, lighter materials for helmets, body armour and aircraft. Its unusual eyes have inspired cameras that detect polarised light, which could help doctors spot cancer cells. In parts of Asia and the Mediterranean, mantis shrimp species are also eaten. Protecting coral reefs, through marine protected areas and limits on destructive fishing, is the best way to safeguard these remarkable animals.

common-eastern-firefly.anatomy: The common eastern firefly is a soft-bodied beetle, about 1 to 1.5 centimetres long, with a black body, pinkish-red and yellow markings on the shield over its head, and wing covers edged with pale yellow. Its light organ is in the last segments of its abdomen, which look pale yellow-green in daylight. Inside, special cells combine a chemical called luciferin with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called luciferase, to make light. Fireflies control the flashes by adjusting the flow of oxygen to these cells. Males have larger light organs than females and big eyes, which help them spot females' answering flashes in the dark. The larvae, sometimes called glowworms, are flattened, segmented and dark, and they glow too, perhaps to warn predators that they taste unpleasant.
common-eastern-firefly.family: On warm summer evenings, males fly low over grass, each flashing a single half-second swoop, rising in a J shape, about every six seconds. Females wait on grass blades or low plants and answer with a flash of their own about two seconds after a male's signal. The male follows the flashes to her. After mating, females lay eggs singly or in clusters in moist soil. The eggs themselves glow faintly. Larvae hatch after a few weeks and live in damp soil and leaf litter for one to two years, hunting snails, slugs and worms by injecting them with digestive enzymes. In spring, a mature larva builds a small chamber of soil, pupates for a couple of weeks, and emerges as an adult in early summer, completing a life lived mostly underground.
common-eastern-firefly.people: Fireflies are among the most beloved insects in North America, linked with childhood memories of catching them in jars on summer nights. The common eastern firefly is the state insect of Tennessee and Pennsylvania. Its luciferase was among the first to be studied in labs, and the enzyme, along with the gene that makes it, is now a common research tool, used to make cells glow so scientists can detect bacteria, track genes and test drugs. Firefly watching has become popular, and in some places, like the Great Smoky Mountains, synchronous fireflies draw so many visitors that viewing is limited by lottery. Conservationists encourage people to turn off outdoor lights, leave patches of long grass and leaf litter, and avoid pesticides on lawns, simple steps that help fireflies thrive.

ruby-throated-hummingbird.anatomy: The ruby-throated hummingbird is tiny, with a long, straight, needle-like bill and a long, forked tongue that laps nectar up to around 13 times a second. Its back is shimmering emerald green. Males have an iridescent throat patch called a gorget that flashes ruby red in the right light and looks black otherwise; females have white throats. Its wings are attached by a flexible shoulder joint that lets them rotate, producing lift on both the forward and backward strokes, so it can hover, fly sideways and even backwards. Flight muscles make up about a quarter to a third of its weight. Its legs and feet are so small that it can barely walk and instead shuffles or flies even short distances. Hummingbirds have excellent colour vision, including ultraviolet, helping them find flowers.
ruby-throated-hummingbird.family: Male ruby-throats arrive on the breeding grounds first and defend feeding areas, performing dramatic U-shaped dive displays in front of females, swooping back and forth with buzzing wings. After mating, the male leaves and plays no part in nesting. The female builds a tiny cup-shaped nest about the size of half a walnut shell on a branch, made of plant down and bound with spider silk, then camouflaged with lichen. She lays two eggs about the size of peas and incubates them for around two weeks. She feeds the chicks a slurry of nectar and insects, pushing her bill deep into their throats. The young leave the nest at about three weeks old. In southern parts of the range, females may raise two broods in a summer.
ruby-throated-hummingbird.people: Ruby-throated hummingbirds are one of the most familiar backyard birds in eastern North America, and millions of people hang feeders to attract them. Experts recommend a simple mix of one part white sugar to four parts water, changed every few days to prevent mould, and warn against red dye, honey or artificial sweeteners. Native flowers such as bee balm, cardinal flower and trumpet honeysuckle provide natural food. Many birdwatchers record the first ruby-throat to arrive in spring and report sightings to citizen science projects such as eBird and Journey North, which map their migration north each year. Bird banders place tiny numbered rings on hummingbirds' legs, revealing that some return to the same feeders year after year and live much longer than expected.

wandering-albatross.anatomy: The wandering albatross is a huge white seabird with black wingtips and a large pink bill. Young birds are dark brown and gradually turn white over many years, so older birds are the whitest; the oldest males are almost entirely white. Its long, narrow wings are ideal for gliding, and a special tendon locks its shoulder joints, holding the wings out without muscle effort. Tube-shaped nostrils on top of its bill give it an excellent sense of smell, which it uses to find food spread across the ocean surface. Glands above its eyes remove salt from the seawater it drinks, and it sneezes out the salty solution through its nostrils. On land it is clumsy, and on calm days it struggles to take off, running into the wind.
wandering-albatross.family: Wandering albatrosses form pair bonds that typically last for life. They return to the same breeding islands and perform elaborate courtship dances, spreading their huge wings, pointing their bills skyward, clapping bills and calling. The pair builds a large mound nest of grass and mud and lays a single egg, which both parents incubate in shifts for around 11 weeks while the other goes to sea to feed. After hatching, the chick is guarded for a few weeks, then left alone on the nest through the harsh subantarctic winter while both parents forage far out at sea, returning to feed it oily meals of squid and fish. The chick fledges after about nine months. It then spends several years at sea before returning to land to breed, usually at around ten years old.
wandering-albatross.people: Albatrosses have inspired sailors for centuries; seeing one was considered good luck, and killing one bad luck, an idea immortalised in Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner'. In the 20th century, many seabird islands were visited by sealers and whalers, and the birds faced new threats from introduced rats and mice, which can attack chicks. The biggest modern danger is longline fishing, where albatrosses grab baited hooks and drown. Since the 2000s, the Albatross Task Force of BirdLife International has worked with fishing crews to adopt simple bird-scaring lines, weighted hooks and night setting, which can cut seabird deaths dramatically. Rat and mouse eradication projects, such as on South Georgia, have also helped. Albatrosses are protected under the international Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels.
